titleStmt.title: De venenatis animalibus eorumque remediis; or, On Venomous Animals and Their Remedies

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise auto-generee (IA, non relue par un helleniste) a partir du texte grec de l'edition critique de Max Wellmann (1908, Corpus Medicorum Graecorum X 1,1, Teubner, Leipzig/Berlin), traite en 37 chapitres transmis par le seul codex Vaticanus gr. 284. L'encodage deja present dans le corpus zoomathia pour ce texte (zoo70/1g) s'est revele inexploitable : son OCR n'a capture de maniere fiable qu'une petite partie du corps du traite (essentiellement le debut du chapitre 1), le reste etant domine par la preface latine de l'edition et par l'index des mots grecs en fin de volume. Cette traduction a donc ete etablie directement a partir des images de page du meme volume (edition Wellmann 1908, exemplaire numerise par la Wellcome Collection, archive.org/details/b23983863, domaine public), lues et transcrites manuellement chapitre par chapitre, en contournant entierement l'OCR defaillant. Seul le texte grec courant du traite a ete traduit ; l'apparat critique (variantes manuscrites, notes des editeurs) en bas de chaque page n'a pas ete repris, non plus que les rares lacunes ou passages corrompus du manuscrit unique (signales dans l'edition Wellmann par des crochets ou des points de suspension), qui sont laisses de cote plutot que combles par conjecture. Le decoupage en 37 chapitres numerotes reprend la table des matieres de l'edition (fol. 264 du manuscrit). Traduction fournie a titre de meilleur effort ; a verifier par un helleniste avant toute citation savante. Correspond au texte grec deja present dans le corpus sous zoo70/1g.

div.head: Signs of a rabid dog, and of those bitten by it
div.p: We have placed the account of those bitten by rabid animals before the others, since the animal is both common and familiar, is continually seized by rabies, and is difficult to guard against, so that the danger from it is severe unless one makes use of many remedies. A dog generally goes rabid in the fiercest heat, but sometimes also in intense cold. Once rabid, it turns away from food and drink, puts forth much foamy phlegm from its mouth, has a wicked look, and is grimmer than usual; it attacks, without barking, all alike, both beasts and men, both familiar and strangers, and its bite produces at first nothing troublesome beyond the pain of the wound, but afterward brings on the affliction called hydrophobia.

This comes with convulsions, derangement, and reddening of the whole body, especially the face, together with sweating and helplessness. Some of those with hydrophobia flee the light, others waste away continually; some, on seeing water or having it offered to them, bark like dogs, and bite anyone who approaches, and, having bitten, become themselves the cause of the same affliction in others. Of those who have fallen into hydrophobia we know of none who recovered, save that we have learned by report of one or two: Eudemus says that a certain man survived it — some say that this man, having been bitten, fell into the affliction and was saved; others say that, having devotedly and sympathetically attended a friend suffering from hydrophobia, he fell into the same condition himself and, after suffering greatly, was saved. The affliction, then, is a grievous one; yet even before putting it to our own test, we ourselves have seen many saved by other physicians, and have known of others who recovered.

div.head: Treatment of a rabid dog's bite
div.p: Of the treatment, one part is general, to be used for anyone bitten by any venomous creature, while another part is peculiar to those bitten by rabid dogs, being wont to help some greatly but unsuited to those bitten a long time before. Having set out this particular remedy first, we shall then run quickly over the general treatment as well.

One should burn river-crabs on white-vine wood and, having ground their ash fine, keep it stored; likewise one should also store away roots of gentian, pounded and sifted. Whenever someone is bitten by a rabid dog, into three or four cups of unmixed wine one should stir a spoonful of the crab-ash and one spoonful of the gentian, and, having mixed it like barley-gruel, give it to the bitten person to drink daily from the first day up to the fortieth; let the wine be rather old than new, and if the patient cannot bear it unmixed, let it be diluted, but kept fairly strong.

The remedy is given in this manner from the start; but if two or three days have already passed since the bite before the treatment is begun, one should make the remedy three times as concentrated, keeping the same measure of wine, and then on the second, third and fourth day return to the ordinary measure stated from the beginning. This, then, is the best remedy for those bitten by rabid animals — one which by itself has sufficed for some — and it should be used with confidence. But so as to be secured also by other means against a danger that otherwise seems inescapable, there is nothing to prevent one from using the remaining remedies too; for it is better, if it comes to that, to endure the harshness of remedies applied needlessly than to fall into danger through neglect.

One should be no less wary of small wounds resembling mere scratches than of large ones: through the larger wounds, since much blood is forced out and flows freely, one can wash the venom away along with it, but through the smaller ones this cannot happen at all; hence with the larger wounds the flesh that comes away of itself should be removed and the edges pared round about, while with the smaller ones a wider area should be marked out with the blade; and once the flesh has been raised, with a hook or a probe, the excision should then be carried out.

In both cases the surrounding area should be scored with fairly deep scratches all around, so that the resulting freer flow of blood may work against the venom's spreading further inward. A cupping-glass applied with a strong flame would also be of great help, so as to draw out the destructive force together with the matter itself.

div.head: On cauterization of wounds from venomous bites
div.p: Cauterization is the most effective remedy of all against venomous wounds: for fire, being more potent than any other force, at once overpowers the venom and prevents it from being carried further inward, and at the same time consumes the part of it it has overpowered; moreover it lays no ordinary foundation for the treatment that follows, since the ulceration persists longer once the scab falls away. One must take particular care that the scars do not close up sooner than forty days, but that the sores be kept, so far as possible, inflamed and irritated for a long while. This effect is produced by applying a very pungent piece of salted fish, and finely-ground garlic soaked in vinegar, and — if pyrethrum is available — chewed and applied, and, more or less by way of general poultices, bran soaked together with vinegar likewise helps, and vinegar by itself helps a great deal. And Straton hands down, as peculiarly his own, the following in his writings: apply bruised bay-leaves, he says, and give the patient bay-leaves to drink mixed with wine, or give Cyrenaic sap to drink likewise, or having mixed pepper with the running juice of the bay-tree give that to drink with rather strong wine, or apply silphium similarly softened with wine.

For those bitten by the moray-eel the same remedies apply as for those bitten by other venomous creatures, and for this reason the same helps should be used. Archigenes says: for bites from sea-creatures — the sting-ray, the moray, the sea-dragon, or from a fig-tree's sap — pour on four or five drops from a bundle of wild thyme, or of a creeping ivy, three or four times.

div.head: On the diet of those bitten by rabid dogs, and on those who fall into hydrophobia despite earlier precautions
div.p: One must also aim the diet against the venom, so that it may at once blunt and quench its power, while also hindering its passage into the depths of the body: for these foods, once taken in, already work against the destructive power's stealing further inward. Each of these effects can be produced by a drink of unmixed and rather strong wine, of sweet wine, and of milk: for all these, moving quickly to the surface of the body, resist the venom and dissolve all its sharpness; and likewise the eating of garlic, onions, and leeks; and these foods, being altogether resistant to change — since their qualities persist for many days — are not overcome or turned aside by the destructive power, but by their contrary nature are naturally able to master it. For this same purpose there is also need of antidotes, such as theriac, the so-called Eupatorium antidote, the Mithridatium, and every other kind compounded from many spices: for all spices are by nature resistant to change, both in their powers and in their substances, and for this reason they master the venoms present in the body. Such, then, is the manner of the diet.

One must know that the onset of the hydrophobic affliction has no single or fixed limit of time; for the most part, when the aforesaid remedies have not been neglected, it strikes around the fortieth day, but it has already occurred in some after six months, and even after a year — this too we ourselves have witnessed. Some record that certain persons have been seized by the affliction even after seven years.

The treatment for those just bitten by rabid dogs has been described above. But if, for whatever reason, the aforesaid remedies were not used in the first days, one should no longer strip away flesh or cauterize: it is futile to try to reach, so late, what has already passed into the depths of the body — no benefit comes of the attempt, and the body is merely subjected to needless pain. A different method of treatment should be introduced instead, aiming to purge the body and change its whole condition, so that the ill habit of body is evacuated and transformed.

Let the sacred remedy made with colocynth be given, and curdled milk, which can at once purge and temper the body; and sharp, pungent foods, which can daily blunt the venom; and the drinking of unmixed wine should be taken daily; and besides these, the inducing of sweat both before and after meals, and pitch-plasters and mustard-plasters applied in turn over the whole body.
Of all things, I have found hellebore to be the most effective remedy in these cases, and it should be used boldly — not once or twice, but repeatedly, both before and after the fortieth day.

So great is the power of this remedy that even some already seized by hydrophobia have been saved by taking hellebore right at the first onset of the symptoms; but for those already fully overcome, neither this nor anything else can save them.

For hydrophobia, the remedy made with rennet: hare's rennet, Lemnian earth, and juniper berries, four drachms of each, bay-berries and myrrh, six drachms of each; work up with honey. The dose is the size of an Egyptian bean. Another: take a dog's vomit, dry it, grind it fine, keep it in a box, and use it with confidence as an excellent remedy for those bitten by rabid dogs.
From the recipe of Theodorus: for those bitten by a rabid dog, tie on as an amulet a root of spurge-olive, using it as a marvellous remedy.

Another, for those bitten by rabid dogs, so that they do not fall into hydrophobia: [an obscure sign is given, concerning the bitten person's own shadow, as is customary in judging the healthy]. A prognosis for the sufferer, whether he will live: make him stare fixedly into a mirror; if he recognizes himself, he will live; if not, he will not — this sign never fails.

From the seventh book of Theodorus: the dog-bite remedy of Crates, by which trial the venom is found, during treatment, in the urine of the one bitten: scraped verdigris and salt, six drachms of each, calf's fat, twelve drachms; grind together and use, sprinkling it onto a compress. Keep the patient's urine in a glass vessel, and you will find in it the proof that the remedy is working.

div.head: On dog-bites and human-bites
div.p: Archigenes, in the fifth book of his work On Remedies by Kind, writes as follows: for those bitten by other humans, first anoint with oil, then apply crushed fennel-root mixed with honey until the wound is cleansed; then take equal parts of myrrh and turpentine-resin and apply as a poultice; or take burnt copper-vitriol worked up with boiled honey, insert it as a pledget, and, having thus cleansed the wound, close it up. From Straton: burn calf's bones until they turn white, work them up with liquid pitch or honey or both, and insert. Another: crush frankincense-manna and apply as a plaster with oil and wine.

On dog-bites. For dog-bites, strike the bite at once, without delay, using the flat of the hand dipped in vinegar; then pour soda mixed with vinegar over it; or knead vetch-meal with oil and apply; or apply a fresh sponge, or greasy unwashed wool soaked in vinegar and oil; or soak a fresh sponge in cold water, or in vinegar-and-water, or in vinegar, and let it lie on the wound for three days, moistening it repeatedly with the liquids named above: this works exceptionally well and heals the wound completely in the end. For bites that have already become purulent, knead vetch-meal with honey and apply: this works excellently.

From the Useful Remedies of Apollonius: for inflamed bites, grind litharge with water and anoint, or apply a poultice of boiled, mashed lentils. Make use also of fasting, purging, and keeping the bitten limb still; or grind up whatever very old salted fish you have and apply it as a plaster — this is more effective than any other remedy. Above all: my teacher makes it still more effective by grinding garlic in with it. So for dog-bites and human-bites, apply a plaster of ground salt mixed with honey, until the wound is filled in. Some also add onion to these remedies along with vinegar, and use it in that form. The same remedies should also be used for human-bites, for they suit the condition of both alike.

From the recipes of Theodorus: burn dog's dung, dissolve it in oil, and apply — it seems to me that leek should also be mixed in with this. Another: burn dry dill, fill the bite-wound with it, and by the fifth day it will heal cleanly. Another: apply cabbage leaves, verdigris, rue, and salt.

div.head: Fumigations against reptiles
div.p: From Archigenes: the hooves and hair of goats, fumigated at a distance, drive away reptiles by their smell. A compound fumigation of Philinus: galbanum, root of restharrow, deer's horn, and black cumin, one pound of each; grind all together and work up with vinegar, making it into lozenges. When needed, soak one in oil and fumigate in the middle of the house; if out of doors, in the middle of the sleeping-place. Another: melt galbanum and mongoose-fat, one pound of each, and steep; when needed, fumigate in the same way. Another, Egyptian remedy: soak a sloughed snakeskin in oil and fumigate near the burrows, and the snakes will come up out of them at once. Another remedy draws out scorpions and drives every reptile from the house: fumigate with copper-vitriol, realgar, butter, bryony, and goat's fat, in equal parts.

div.head: Ointments against reptiles
div.p: Let the body be anointed all over with oil in which fresh cedar-shavings have been steeped, or juniper berries, fleabane, sulphurwort, silphium, sage, wild mallow, southernwood, cardamom, larkspur, wild-carrot seed, or galbanum; and with sulphurwort-sap diluted with vinegar, or with oil-and-vinegar, or with compounds made from these.
As a general remedy against every wild creature, the fat of each kind, smeared on, drives away its own kind by the smell — just as a dog, on smelling a crushed tick of its own kind, quickly flees.

Remedies for those struck by wild creatures: if someone is struck by a venomous beast and the venom remains mild, pour warm water or vinegar-and-water over the wound and suck it out. The one performing the suction must not be fasting, but should have eaten and rinsed his mouth with wine, and, keeping a little oil in his mouth, should then perform the suction in that way.

Care must be taken that the mouth, teeth, or tonsils of the one sucking out the venom are not themselves harmed. After this, ash mixed with vinegar and applied helps — especially ash of fig-wood, bay-wood, or vine-wood; failing that, whatever is at hand, taking care above all not to provoke inflammation. If the wound is more severe, scarification should also be used, with fairly deep scratches, so that the matter may be drawn up from deep within.

Cupping-glasses should also be used, to draw the matter up from deep within; stripping away flesh and excision help even more than scarification. And if the bitten part is well suited to removal, amputation should be performed without hesitation, above all in the case of any venomous beast, as with the asp, the horned viper, and the like.

Ground salted fish, leeks, onions and garlic — sometimes ground fine and applied as a poultice, sometimes burnt and applied to the bite; or split birds wrapped around the struck spot, since the warmth of the animal draws out the breath, and with it the venom, from the bitten part; calamint applied as a poultice also helps, as does garlic with salt, and goat's dung.

Above all effective against the bite of any venomous creature except the asp is quicklime mixed with oil and honey, applied to the thickness of a wax-salve until a scab forms; or grind salt fine and apply as a plaster with liquid pitch. We have learned that something of this kind is done in Egypt: whenever the Egyptians are reaping, they keep a pot of boiling pitch ready, with a bandage attached to it. Whenever someone is bitten on the shin or the hand, those nearby quickly throw the bandage into the boiling pitch and wind it once or twice around the forearm or shin a little above the bite; two men standing by pull it tight forcefully, cutting into the spot as the tourniquet is applied, and then cauterize it.

When it seems to them that this has been done enough, they remove the tourniquet and apply a poultice of onions, or one of the other things mentioned, made up as a plaster of liquid pitch with fairly warm ground salt; renewing it fairly often helps a great deal. Pouring vinegar and seawater in which calamint has been boiled over the wound also helps. There are also very pungent plasters able to draw out the venom, hold it, and disperse it, such as the one made with salt, or with soda and restharrow together.

The following, too, should be mentioned: chicory, heath, and vetch drunk with vinegar help all those bitten by wild beasts; likewise asphalt, and green plane-tree balls boiled in wine-and-water, a decoction of Christ's-thorn, the root of birthwort, boiled bay-berries eaten, dill, garlic, onions, and very pungent salted fish, a decoction of marjoram drunk with wine, and the juice of fennel, pennyroyal, calamint and leek, sipped with honey-water.

These remedies are drawn from plants; but useful things are also taken from animals: hens' brains eaten; hare's rennet drunk with wine; castoreum likewise, in the same measure. Among the celebrated remedies too is the weasel, prepared as a skeleton: it is first singed over a flame after its innards have been removed, then dried in the shade down to a skeleton, and a two-drachm dose of it is given with wine.

Purging by the bowels and inducing sweat through copious excretion also suit those bitten by wild beasts. The following prepared draughts are more commonly handed down for the bites of most venomous creatures: opium and myrrh, one obol of each, pepper, one drachm, birthwort, two drachms — worked up with honey and given, in the size of an Egyptian bean, with wine; likewise wild-rue seed, Ethiopian cumin, galbanum, black cumin, and birthwort, all ground fine and kneaded with rocket-juice into one-drachm lozenges, of which a half-cotyle is given with wine; or two drachms of gentian, with a sufficient quantity of pepper and rue, ground and given with wine.
So much for the remedies held in common; the remedies peculiar to each of the venomous creatures we shall discuss next in turn.

div.head: For those bleeding from a wound inflicted by a wild beast
div.p: For bleeding from such wounds, one should give the styptic remedy of Hermas the beast-doctor: copper ore, black vitriol, and spiders' webs, one pound of each, ground together — use this.

div.head: On diet and treatment, in general
div.p: One should use pungent foods, easily digested, wind-producing and sharp-tasting — such as garlic, onions, salted fish, pepper, and radishes — and wine in quantity, unmixed. All manner of movement and much gentle rocking, by day and by night, is beneficial to such patients.

div.head: Theriac antidotes and plasters, effective also against other things
div.p: The first antidote, effective in general against all venomous creeping creatures and against rabid-dog bites, called by many the 'four-ingredient' remedy. The dose of the drug is the size of a Pontic nut; for those stung by scorpions, give it with dry wine once a day — and if the pain intensifies, give it twice — but for those bitten by rabid dogs give it with water every other day for forty-two days, mixing into the drug some Indian lycium, and taking care that the wounds do not close up. Use it dry, if you wish, on the wounds too. Its ingredients are round birthwort, gentian, bay-berries, and myrrh, eight drachms of each, worked up with Attic or boiled honey. If four drachms of white pepper are added, it also works wonderfully for liver ailments taken with hydromel, and during attacks taken with sweet wine.

Another theriac antidote, of exceptional power. Its ingredients are castoreum, Cyrenaic sap, and pepper, four drachms of each; costus, Indian spikenard, saffron, and centaury-juice, two drachms of each; half a cotyle of skimmed honey. The dose is the size of a Pontic nut; it is given to those stung by scorpions with mixed wine, to those bitten by asps with mixed vinegar, to those with liver ailments with hydromel, likewise for suffocating fits of the womb; to bring on the menses, give it after the bath with warm honeyed wine.

Another antidote for those stung by scorpions: give one spoonful of finely-ground long birthwort with four cups of unmixed wine — it works powerfully. Another theriac antidote for scorpion-stings: give a fine-ground decoction of four gourds of long birthwort with unmixed wine — highly effective.

On plasters. Zeno of Laodicea, after his own theriac antidote — which I have not set down here on account of the costliness of its preparation — appends the following plasters, saying as follows: for bites, apply the plaster made with seawater, or the white one, or a mixture of both.

The one made with chamaeleon-thistle is this: one pound and two ounces of litharge, one drachm of ammoniac salt, four ounces of the root of black chamaeleon-thistle, three cotyles of seawater, one pint of old oil. Boil the litharge, oil, and seawater until it thickens, then remove from the fire, add the ground chamaeleon-root, sprinkle it in, and cook over a gentle fire, so that the chamaeleon-root imparts its power to the remedy.

Another, the white plaster: one pound of white lead, one pound of pine-resin, seven pounds of old oil, six pounds of wax, and two pounds each of ammoniac gum-resin and galbanum. Boil the oil, white lead and litharge until it no longer stains; then add the rest afterward, and use it for every kind of abscess and swelling of the breasts, boils, fistulous swellings, sinuses, tumours behind the ear, and carbuncles. Use both of these plasters alike for bites. This latter causes no inflammation against any venom, and this recipe has never before been published.

div.head: On wasps and bees
div.p: I shall first explain the signs that accompany the stings of these creatures — not because their power is great or their sting dangerous, but so that those stung may not be alarmed by the pain, as though struck by one of the more dangerous creatures.

Those stung by bees experience the following: the sting-site is painful, the area is red, the surrounding parts swell up, and the sting itself remains lodged in the wound; those stung by wasps have the same symptoms, except that the sting is not left behind.

Such stings are helped by applying mud kneaded with vinegar-and-water; or mallow-leaves ground together with vinegar-and-water in the same way; or barley-meal with vinegar; or fig-sap dripped onto the sting; or ground heliotrope-leaves sprinkled on; or grind sesame itself with water and apply as a plaster.

One should also stamp the sting-site at once with an iron seal-ring, to prevent the swelling from increasing; steaming with brine or seawater also helps. Give the patient beforehand about two drachms of tender bay-leaves to drink with about half a cotyle of dry wine.

div.head: On flies, gnats, and fleas
div.p: Since these too plague the bodies of men, I shall write a little about them as well. Gnats die when cedar-shavings mixed with copper-vitriol are burnt as a fumigant beneath them; and if black-cumin is boiled in oil, mixed with copper-vitriol, and used to anoint the body, not even gnats will come near.

To kill flies: grind henbane seed, black hellebore, and litharge together with water, and store it away; when needed, mix saffron-flower with butter and the ground root of dog's-mercury together with fat, in equal parts, boil with oil, and anoint the surface with it; or fumigate with dried substances burnt on cow-dung.

Another remedy against gnats: anoint with Syrian resin mixed with vinegar. Another: anoint with hellebore and wormwood in radish-oil. Fumigated copper-vitriol drives away flies; copper-vitriol ground fine and mixed with milk, and set out in various places, also drives them away.

Deadly to fleas: the decoction of oleander boiled in seawater or brine, sprinkled about. Another, for killing off gnats and fleas together: fumigate with frankincense and black cumin. Another: soak the root of the Egyptian bean in water and sprinkle it about.

div.head: For the bite of a gecko
div.p: Those bitten by a gecko suffer intense pain, and the bite-wound turns livid. They are helped by at once applying a poultice of onions and garlic to the wound, and also by eating these same things and drinking unmixed wine; or grind sesame with water and apply as a plaster, or black cumin in the same way.

div.head: Amulets and antipathic remedies for a scorpion's sting, and other help against the same
div.p: From Archigenes: there are many kinds of scorpions, but the same symptoms follow from all of them, and so I shall turn to the signs of their stings and to the treatments. Those stung experience very severe pain around the sting, chill and numbness over the whole body, cold sweat, and swelling in the armpits, or, in those stung lower down, in the groin.

In those struck more severely, the following symptoms follow: a burning heat around the sting as though scorched by fire, derangement and throbbing throughout the whole body, a prickling like ants crawling over the lips and the whole body, so that one seems sprinkled with poppy-juice, stiffness of the joints, distortion of the face, a sticky discharge gathering around the eyes, thick tears, continuous shivering, thickness and hardness of the tongue, continuous chattering of the teeth, copious foaming at the mouth, vomiting, hiccuping, convulsions, tetanus, and backward-arching spasms.

The following remedies help at once: fig-sap dripped into the wound; or — by a kind of antipathy — the very scorpion that stung the patient, applied to the wound, which helps exceedingly well; or ground salt with linseed; or the fruit of marsh-mallow; or unfired sulphur worked up with turpentine-resin and applied as a plaster; or galbanum spread flat in the shape of a compress; or ground calamint applied as a poultice with water; and coarse-ground barley prepared in wine with a decoction of rue; or the grime scraped from a vessel, smeared on; or the root of birthwort; or apply a poultice of salt with raisins, or rub in ground salt with oil.

Very effective draughts should also be used: two drachms of birthwort, especially the bark, with wine; crushed gentian with pennyroyal added; ten bay-berries, ground fine; calamint boiled for a long time in vinegar-and-water; cypress with wine, or rue likewise, and silphium if it is available, or the seed of trefoil-cypress, drunk, and basil-seed; repeated bathing accompanied by copious sweating; and drinking wine mixed rather strong.
A tried antidote for scorpion-stings: long birthwort, black cumin, root of all-heal, and wild-rue seed, four drachms of each; the dose is two drachms with unmixed wine.

Another, effective also against tertian, quartan, and daily recurring fevers: opium, the juice of all-heal, castoreum, henbane seed, and wild-carrot seed, one drachm of each, ground fine; mix in a little honey and give three drachm-weights to a man, half that to children; use it for scorpion-stings without honeyed wine, an hour before the dose is taken.

Those stung by a scorpion are given the root of the olive-tree to chew, until the pain leaves them; and if one has this on hand, the scorpion will do no harm. Whoever carries a gecko about with him will not be stung. Another remedy against being stung by a scorpion: six flowers of valerian, a little black cumin, and a little propolis — mix these, bind them into a woollen cloth, and wear as an amulet. And if you wish to test this, draw a circle on the ground and place a scorpion in the middle together with the amulet, and the scorpion will not come out of the circle.

div.head: How many kinds of spiders there are, and remedies against them
div.p: There are many kinds of spiders, but those most precisely recorded by the writers on venomous creatures number six in all: one is called the grape-spider, another the wolf, another the ant-spider, another the skull-pecker, another the hard-head, and another the worm-spider.

The grape-spider is round in shape and black in colour — for it resembles the grape of a black cluster — and has very tiny legs on each side, with its mouth beneath its belly. The wolf, the second kind, is found living among cobwebs, catching flies and eating them; it has a broad, rounded body, markings grooved around its neck, and three smooth projections from its mouth.

The ant-spider, the third kind, resembles a large ant and is sooty in colour; marks like stars are imprinted on its body, especially along its back, as Nicander attests, saying: "fiery, its form resembled a dried husk, speckled all over its broad back as with stars."

The hard-head, the fourth kind, has a rocky, hardened head, and over its whole body is patterned like the moths that fly around lamps. The worm-spider, the fifth, is elongated and dusky, especially about the head. The sixth, the skull-pecker, has an elongated neck, and, falling upon its victim, strikes at the regions of the head.

These, then, are the kinds of spiders; the symptoms that follow in those stung by any of them are common to all: the bite itself is slight and hard to make out; there is swelling, a livid discoloration, and in some also redness; chill about the knees and shoulder-blades; sometimes a heaviness over the whole body, together with severe pain, trembling, loss of colour, and sleeplessness; in some also an erection of the penis and itching around the sting, sometimes also around the shins; watery, tearful eyes, sunken from the belly's uneven swelling.
The whole body swells, the face and especially the region of the tongue most of all; speech becomes indistinct, and in some there is also difficulty urinating, and vomiting.

Watery discharges too occur, resembling cobwebs; sometimes the same matter is passed through the urine and the bowels. Often there is trembling through the whole body, a tension about the backs of the knees resembling cramp, severe gnawing pain about the stomach, and cold sweat breaking out over the whole surface of the body.

When patients are placed in hot water they become free of pain, but once they come out they suffer intense pain again; in older patients the affected parts remain slack for a good while and cannot be made taut. These are the symptoms common to all; but in some there is also headache and dimming of vision, and when the skull-pecker spider has struck, there follows severe shivering, as though being beaten, heartburn, and restless tossing about.

All those bitten by spiders are helped by frequent hot baths, and the wound should be bathed with a decoction of trefoil and warm oil. Apply fig-ash mixed with ground salt and wine, or birthwort with barley-meal soaked in vinegar. Bathe the sores with rather hot seawater or brine, and with a decoction of balm — whose leaves should also be applied as a poultice — or with squills, leeks, or bran boiled up in vinegar, or barley-meal boiled together with bay-leaves in wine; or dip a fresh sponge in vinegar and foment the wound with it.

Give the patient to drink southernwood-seed, dill, birthwort, wild chickpea, Ethiopian cumin, ground cedar-berries, plane-tree bark, and the seed of trefoil-grass — two drachms of each separately in a single cotyle. Likewise also the fruit of tamarisk and the leaves of ground-pine, and a decoction of green cypress-balls mixed with wine, or one drachm of ground pellitory drunk the same way.

Some also say that a river-crab, crushed into juice with milk, with the addition of celery-seed, relieves the troublesome symptoms at once. Or grind pepper in a cotyle of wine to a moderate thickness and give it to drink.

div.head: How many kinds of asps there are
div.p: According to the writers on venomous creatures there are three kinds of asps: some are called land-asps, others swallow-asps, and others are named spitting-asps; these differ from one another in size, colour, and effect. The land-asps are found up to three cubits long, sometimes even five, and their effects are proportionate to their length.

The spitting-asps, the largest of them, reach two cubits; the swallow-asps resemble them, whence their name. The spitting-asps are ash-coloured, greenish, and shot with gold; the land-asps too are found sometimes ash-coloured, sometimes greenish.

Common to all bitten by them are puncture-marks at the bite, like those of a needle, two or four in number — and, if it is a female asp, without any pain, should the creature happen to detach itself without being pulled away. There follow also numbness, pallor of the face, chill, slack and repeated drooping of the eyelids, a tilting of the neck, heaviness of the head, sluggishness, a drowsy stupor, an unvarying pulse, and, toward the end, convulsions.

Death occurs within two or three hours from the land-asp, and even sooner from the swallow-asp. Those spat upon by the spitting-asp suffer dimming of sight, swelling of the face, and loss of hearing, with a light pain that is not without a certain pleasure — for which reason Nicander well said: "the man perishes without struggle." The complexion becomes fixed and pale-green, there is slight heartburn, the forehead is continually drawn upward, and the eyelids grow motionless with a loss of sensation resembling sleep — and along with these symptoms death carries the victim off, within less than a third of a day.

Those struck by any of these are helped by prompt amputation, if the bitten part allows it; otherwise the flesh must be stripped away and cut out deeply, down to the bone, so that the affected tissue is removed, and what remains must be dried out with cauterization.

Simple remedies too should be used at once: give very sharp vinegar to drink, until the patient reacts to its taste, for the venom of these creatures congeals the blood and breath in the arteries with great speed, just as that of the basilisk does. Apply centaury ground together with myrrh and opium to the wound. Another: grind mustard with linseed in vinegar and apply.

To know whether the stricken person will live: grind centaury with wine and give it to him; if he vomits it up, he will die of the affliction; if not, he will be saved. And to counter the unpleasant sensation and stomach upset caused by the antidote, grind garlic and give with beer until it settles, or give the juice of all-heal with wine-and-water, and it will act at once.

Numenius the writer on venomous creatures says: grind Heraclean marjoram, whether dried or fresh, to the required strength, and give with wine; along with this theriac antidote, one should also use the general remedies described at the beginning.

div.head: The viper and the adder
div.p: In those bitten by a viper or adder we find two or four puncture-marks, but wider than those of an asp, from which blood is discharged first, then a bloody, oily, bile-tinged serum; a fiery, blistering, reddish swelling appears, then turns livid and spreads; the mouth becomes utterly dry; there is a burning sensation, prostration, a shivering that runs through the body, sometimes vomiting of bile, colic, heaviness of the head and loins, and dizziness with darkened vision.
Pallor, hiccuping, fever, rapid breathing, a leaden complexion, cold sweat. Death occurs within seven days, most often on the third, especially in those harmed by the adder.

These bites too are helped by goat's dung ground fine with wine and applied as a poultice, and bay-leaves likewise, and southernwood, and galbanum thrown on in place of a compress, and fresh marjoram ground fine; also the chicks of birds, split open and applied at once while still warm; or vetch-meal kneaded with wine, and roasted squill and crushed camomile, after first bathing the wound with warm water.

Anoint too with bay-leaves and oil and with barley-groats and wild mallow, and apply a poultice of beet-root with barley-groats and vinegar, or iris with barley-groats, or lime with oil, or roasted salt with hyssop, or marjoram with honey. When blisters rise, poultices must be stopped, so as not to strip off the skin; and once the fluid runs out, bathe with warm water for a long time, since patients bathed only briefly fare worse.
After this, treat the swelling and blisters with a plaster of boiled, mashed lentils mixed with honey, until they heal.

Before the swelling develops, let the patient drink wild-rue seed with sweet wine mixed in; and, eating plenty of good salted fish with bread and drinking further quantities of unmixed wine, let him get thoroughly through it; and afterward let him drink birthwort mixed in sweet wine.
Some tie on fine-leaved plants as amulets and promise that they will help.

This works well for such cases: pound crabs together with a good quantity of barley-meal thoroughly in a mortar, mix in some calamint and a little salt, form into lozenges, and dry them; use as a plaster with milk, and give one lozenge to drink with honey-water; or give radish-peel to eat with honey; or give two drachms of ground costus to drink with wine.

Polyeides the writer on venomous creatures says: let the one bitten chew the herb alkibiadion and swallow the juice, applying the chewed residue to the wound; even if someone is at the point of death and uses it this way, he will be saved.

From the Useful Remedies of Apollonius: grind fresh quicklime, soak it in wine, and, once softened, apply as a plaster — most useful for any swelling. Or thoroughly grind fresh goat's dung, first boiled with wine, and apply as a plaster: this is the strongest of all such poultices.

It also works against erysipelas. If someone eats a drachm of black cumin, he will not die. A well-regarded remedy for viper-bites: myrrh, castoreum, pepper, purslane-flower, and half an oxybaphon of its seed — grind all these in sweet Cretan wine, or some other choice wine.

Erasistratus wrote much on remedies for viper-bites, but says the most tried are these: the brains of birds, drunk in wine, help, as does the root of all-heal boiled together with unmixed wine; an oxybaphon of cultivated cabbage-seed, ground fine and drunk with wine, is also good; and it is also good to dip a finger in liquid pitch, then rinse it off into wine and drink the wine.

div.head: The cerastes (horned viper)
div.p: The cerastes, as the writers on venomous creatures relate, is one cubit in size, or, the larger kind, two cubits; in colour it is sand-hued, tapering thin toward the tail; on its head it has two projections resembling horns, from which it got the name cerastes ('horned one'). The scales of its belly are arranged in rows, so that, as it moves, it produces a sound like a hiss from the friction against the sand; it moves sideways rather than in a straight line.

In those bitten by it, a hard swelling rises, and a wine-coloured or blackening serum flows out; the whole area of the bite becomes varicose-like; there is an erection of the genitals; the mind becomes deranged; and dimming of sight follows in most cases; those struck by it may linger on for as long as nine days.

Amputation is suitable for these bites too, if the bitten part allows it; otherwise flesh should be stripped away down to the bone and cauterization performed. They are helped by the same poultices and draughts described for viper-bites; specifically for these, give castoreum with honey-water to drink, or Cyrenaic sap with honey-water. Also anoint together with oil and castoreum; and apply, as a plaster, ground salt worked up with cedar-resin, together with ground weasel-bane mixed with vinegar.

One must pour raw remedies over the bite, and, after making the patient drink much water, force him to vomit; then, after the vomiting, he should first be given a little Ethiopian cumin or myrrh to drink and should rest a while; then radishes should again be given, and much mixed wine drunk all at once, and vomiting induced again; after the vomiting, the crushed leaves of marjoram with wine should be given.
Let the patient also eat salted meat with dry bread and drink wine, until the cause is carried off through urination. Poultices should be applied quite frequently.

div.head: Prester-bites and other 'herpes'-bites
div.p: The same Apollonius, in his Useful Remedies, hands down to us remedies for prester-bites and for 'herpes'-bites; I did not find these kinds of creatures discussed among the writers on venomous animals, but I shall set down the remedies alone, as I found them in Apollonius.

They are these: for prester-bites, apply spider-web and boiled barley-groats as a poultice, or boiled vine-leaves with honey; let the patient eat raw salted fish, drink rather unmixed wine, and induce vomiting. For 'herpes'-bites, the wound should be bathed with plenty of warm water, treated with a poultice of barley-meal boiled with vinegar, and the patient given mixed wine or vinegar to drink.

div.head: The dipsas (the 'thirst-snake')
div.p: The dipsas is called by some writers on venomous creatures the 'burning snake.' It is one cubit in size, tapering from thick to thin; its whole body is marked with black and tawny spots, and it has a very narrow head.

In those bitten by it, along with the bite there follow swelling and a firm, resistant inflammation — symptoms it shares with other bites. But because of it the sufferer grows increasingly ravenous, burning intensely and taking in ever more drink, yet excreting nothing through urine, sweat, or vomit. They perish for one of two reasons: either overcome by thirst, if they take no drink, or, if they take too much, from excessive distension — either low in the groin or at the belly, as happens with dropsical patients who burst from an overflow of fluid.

These too are helped by the remedies described for viper-bites, as Apollonius records in his Useful Remedies, though Straton's work has nothing on the dipsas. As we found among the writers on venomous creatures, it is said that diuretic remedies should specifically be used for these bites, such as a decoction of celery, spikenard, cinnamon, and the like; and, after giving the patient oil, he should be made to vomit. Enemas should also be used.

In vigorous patients bloodletting too should be undertaken; on the affected parts, quicklime with oil applied as a poultice is beneficial, and other drawing remedies may fittingly be used, such as the salt-plaster, the bay-berry plaster, the white plaster, and those described for dog-bites.

div.head: The haemorrhous
div.p: These creatures are sand-coloured, three palms in size, tapering to a small point at the tail; they crawl slowly in a straight line, and their whole body is adorned with many white and black spots; they are also said to be covered with very rough scales. The female crawls with her belly against the ground, her vent set low near the tail; in the male it is near the belly.

These bites are followed by a bloody, discoloured wound turning black, discharging nothing but a little watery fluid; pain in the stomach; difficulty breathing; bleeding through the nostrils and from the opening of the bite, and from whatever other orifices the body has, which burst and bleed. These are the symptoms in the case of the male; with the female haemorrhous, in addition, the corners of the eyes bleed, the gums bleed, blood flows from the teeth and from the roots of the nails, and, in short, throughout the entire body. It also happens that the bleeding, once it sets in, causes the nails to fall out.

One must first attend to stopping the bleeding, then treat the bite with a poultice of boiled vine-leaves with honey, or purslane-leaves with barley-groats. For those recently bitten, before blood appears in the urine, give plenty of garlic and much mixed wine, and force vomiting; then plenty of fish ground with garlic and oil should be given, with bread and much diluted wine; sweet raisins should be eaten in quantity, and, after giving wine again, vomiting should once more be induced.

After the vomiting, fish grilled over coals should be given, and the bladder fomented with many sponges. From Straton: give the white of an egg with honeyed wine, or radish-seed with wine. Apply as a poultice ground salt worked up with liquid pitch.

div.head: The ammodytes and the myagros
div.p: The ammodytes is found to be one cubit in size — it grows no larger — and sand-coloured; its body is marked with black spots, and it has a rather hard tail, split at the tip. It is also called by some the kechrias. It also has rather broad jaws.
In those struck by it, it generally follows that they perish swiftly. The creature itself attacks fearsomely by coiling up, whence it also got its name.

It happens to those struck that they vomit, and a serous discharge comes from the wound; after a little while the serum flows again. Heaviness of the head and fainting also follow. Erasistratus says that the liver, bladder and colon of such patients are affected, for on dissection these parts are found to be somehow damaged. They die within three days; some linger until the seventh. Death comes more swiftly when the bite is from a female of the creature.

These too are helped first by the general remedies, likewise by tying off, scarification, the application of cupping-glasses, and paring around the affected spot. Specifically for these, it helps to drink pennyroyal with oxymel, and castoreum and cinnamon likewise; two drachms of centaury-root with three cups of wine, or the root of birthwort in the same way.

Cress and gentian help similarly. As for the affected spot, treat it with a poultice of lettuce-seed with linseed, or wild or cultivated rue, or wild thyme ground together with asphodel; easily-digested, nourishing foods should be given.
As I found noted elsewhere, the treatment and remedies for the cerastes and the ammodytes are in some way shared with those for the seps, for the symptoms of the three kinds are similar.

In addition to what has been said, wormwood also helps, its juice drunk with three or four cups of water; and the Mithridatium antidote too, if available, should be given; the previously described remedies should also be used, especially the one made with centaury-juice and Cyrenaic sap. Dry black ink applied to the sores also helps, and boiled, mashed lentils with honey and pomegranate-rind, applied as a poultice, are suitable. The same symptoms follow with the myagros too, and it is treated with the same remedies.

div.head: The seps (the creature)
div.p: The creature called the seps is found to be two cubits in size, tapering from thick to thin. It is placid and slow-moving, has a broad head and a sharp-pointed mouth; its whole body is sprinkled with white spots. In those bitten by it, blood is discharged from the visible puncture-marks, and after a little while a foul-smelling serum, along with swelling and a dull, sluggish pain.
The affected parts, becoming putrid, turn white; a scabby, blotchy discolouration comes over the whole body, along with loss of hair over the whole body. Death occurs within three or four days.

These are helped by the remedies described for scorpion- and ammodytes-bites, and Apollonius, in his Useful Remedies, sets down the following for them: anoint the bitten spot with butter and honey. Give the patient to drink the lees of fresh honey-water, with vinegar added and strained off; or oxymel; or boiled fennel-seed with half a cotyle of white wine; or a moderate amount of all-heal root likewise with wine.
It also helps, according to Straton, to give as much purslane-juice as possible to drink, or to give rather strong myrtle-wine, or to grind vine-tendrils with wine and vinegar and give to drink.

div.head: The hydros and the chersydros
div.p: This snake is named as follows: it lives at first in watery places and is called hydros; afterward it moves to quite dry places, and takes its name according to the place it occupies — so, dwelling on dry land, it is called chersydros ('land-and-water snake'). At that stage it becomes more dangerous than it was before: for while in watery places, feeding on moist nourishment, its venom is not undiluted; but once it becomes a land-creature, its venom is at its purest, and more dangerous.
It resembles a small land-asp, except that it cannot spread its neck — a distinctive feature only the asps possess.

In those bitten by them, the wound spreads and swelling occurs, with continuous, burning pain; the spot turns livid and the colour of wine-lees; there is dizziness, prostration, helplessness, and vomiting of foul-smelling bile. Peculiar to this bite is a disordered movement over the whole body, so that something unnatural is even carried down through the bowels, together with a burning sensation over the whole body. Death occurs by the third day at the latest; recovery from the affliction takes time and is achieved only with difficulty.

These too are helped by the general remedies, and specifically by the following: first by the theriac antidotes described above, and further by these: cypress-fruit and myrtle-berry, one drachm of each — pound together, grind fine, and give to drink with hydromel or honeyed wine; or two drachms of birthwort in wine-and-water or vinegar-and-water; or horehound-juice, or a decoction of either with wine; or fresh honeycomb with vinegar. On the affected parts apply quicklime ground with oil, or marjoram mixed with water, or the bark of oak-root ground fine and mixed with barley-meal and honey. The other drawing remedies may also be used.

div.head: On the dryinos ('oak-snake')
div.p: The snakes called dryinoi abound especially around the Hellespont; they lurk among the roots of oak-trees, whence their name. They are foul-smelling, and so, even unseen, are recognized by their presence wherever they are; they are about two cubits long, quite fat, and their whole body is covered with very rough scales; among these scales, it is said, bronze-winged flies lurk, and these flies kill the snakes.

In those bitten by these there follow: a blackening swelling, severe pain, spreading ulceration, derangement, dryness of the body, hiccuping, vomiting of bile, suppression of urine, loss of voice, stupor, trembling, and a violent death. In those who merely tread on it, there is stripping of the skin of the legs and swellings; and generally, from mortification of the bitten area, death follows for most; so potent is the venom that it even harms the hands of the physicians who treat it.
These too are helped by birthwort drunk with wine, and trefoil-grass, and asphodel-root taken in the same way; and the fruit of any kind of oak, drunk and applied as a poultice, helps.
These too are helped by the remedies described for viper-bites, and by some of the general and universal remedies, applied in proportion to the symptoms that follow in those struck.

div.head: On the kenchrines, also called akontias
div.p: The kenchrines snake is two cubits in size, tapering from thick to thin, greenish in colour, especially on the belly, so that it resembles millet in colour, whence some have called it kenchrias. Others say it is not named for this reason, but because it becomes especially vigorous when the millet is in flower. In defending itself it darts forward like a thrown javelin and strikes in that way, whence it has also been named akontias, 'javelin-snake.'

In those bitten by it follow the same symptoms as in viper-bites, but even more severe, so that putrefaction and wasting of the flesh also follow, and their death comes on more terribly too. The remedies are the same as those for viper-bites and for the other, related creatures that produce similar afflictions.

div.head: The amphisbaena and the scytale
div.p: These creatures resemble one another: the body is not drawn from thick to a tapering point, but is of even thickness throughout, so that onlookers cannot tell at which end the head is and at which the tail. The amphisbaena differs from the scytale only in being able to move in both directions, whence it has been called amphisbaena, 'going both ways.'

In those struck by these, the bite appears faint, as though from the sting of a fly; the bite does not kill, but only brings on inflammation, as with wasps and bees, and so the same remedies used for those should be applied here too, and further those described for the chersydros.

Soranus records that the Chalcedonian scytale produces symptoms in those it bites similar to those following a viper's bite, and so the same remedies should be used. And, to put it simply and generally, for the bite of every one of the named kinds of venomous creature, the remedies for viper-bites are suitable, being well-fitted, in general, for the bite of any venomous creature whatsoever.

div.head: The pelias and the elops
div.p: I did not find, among the writers on venomous creatures, a description of these creatures themselves, but I shall record what follows in those struck by them, and the treatments, as I found them.

In those bitten by the pelias there occurs pain around the site and a putrefaction that is not dangerous, together with pain and dimming of vision in the eyes, as the venom rises up into them. They are treated by pouring stale vinegar or brine into the eyes, or by washing the head of an unblemished boy and pouring that wash into the eyes; or by mixing opobalsam with Attic honey, or euphorbium likewise, and anointing with it.

Sharp eye-salves smeared beneath the eyes are also suitable here: by irritating the eyes they open up the passages, and along with the flow of tears the venom is discharged. When the deeper pains have subsided and only the pain around the eyes remains, one must then move on to gentle, soothing eye-salves; beforehand, give the patient barley-gruel with oil to drink.

In those bitten by the elops there follows a colic resembling intestinal obstruction. Those bitten by this creature are treated with the general remedies, especially diuretics and remedies that soothe colic.

div.head: The agathodaimon and the typhlias
div.p: For these too, likewise, a description of their appearance is not found among the writers on venomous creatures. What follows in those struck is this: in those bitten by the agathodaimon, pain alone; in those bitten by the typhlias, pain together with a burning sensation; and so they should be treated with the corresponding remedies.

div.head: The drakon (great serpent)
div.p: This creature is not venomous, but kills by its strength and power. Such serpents abound especially in Ethiopia and in Lycia, and differ in colour: some are black, others tawny, others ash-grey; they also differ greatly in size — some are five cubits, some ten, some fifteen, some twenty, some thirty; even larger ones are recorded.

They are covered in scales over the whole body, have large, fiery eyes, and above these certain crests resembling eyebrows; beneath the chin they have an outgrowth which is called the 'beard.' The gape of their mouths is wide, the tongue protrudes, and the teeth are large, resembling those of wild boars; wherever they bite, they cause fractures. Treatment for their bite should therefore be carried out as for an ordinary wound, not as for the bite of a venomous creature.

div.head: The basilisk
div.p: This creature is three palms in size, sharp-headed, and yellow in colour; and it has the greatest power of all reptiles, so that not one of them can bear even its hiss, but even if some creature is intent on food or drink and becomes aware of it...
...of the wild beast's presence in that place, it turns back and withdraws to where it came from, giving no thought even to the food necessary for life — so great is its power.

In those bitten by it there follows a burning of the whole body and a livid discolouration from the excessive heat of the venom; the hair falls out from the body, so that one struck by it has scarcely any span of life left; moreover, not even a single flesh-eating creature will touch the body of one who has died from it.

If any creature should attack it out of hunger, death overtakes that creature there on the spot as well; and so we consider it futile and superfluous to set down remedies, since none of those struck by it can be saved at all. Erasistratus, however, says that three drachms of castoreum drunk with wine help, and likewise poppy-juice.

div.head: The parôos, the spathiouros, and the centipede
div.p: The parôos snake is found in the regions of Syria. In colour, some are bronze-hued, others blackish; their bite does not kill, but, like the amphisbaena and the scytale, this creature too, when it strikes, brings on only inflammation, and so those struck by it should be treated with the same remedies.

The spathiouros is found in the regions of Chalcis. This creature tapers from thick to thin toward the tail and has a broad head; it is a great enemy of the mouse. It too does not kill when it bites, but only brings on inflammation, and so those struck by it should likewise be treated with similar remedies.

In those bitten by a centipede there follows itching, moderate swelling, and pain that resolves quickly, and so these too are helped by the common remedies. Apollonius, in his Useful Remedies, advises bathing the site with sharp, hot vinegar-brine and applying a poultice of ground salt with vinegar.

div.head: The shrew
div.p: The shrew is likened, in colour, to the domestic weasel, and in size to a mouse, whence it also has its compound name. It is ash-coloured, has an elongated mouth, and a thin, rough tail; it has fine teeth arranged in a double row along each jaw, so that there are four rows of teeth in all.

In those bitten by it the wounds become clearly visible, since marks from four rows of teeth will be seen; blood is discharged first, pure, then after a little while serous, for this creature kills through putrefaction. Blisters also customarily rise up, and if these are stripped away, the flesh beneath is seen to be the colour of wine-lees and torn.

Swelling with wind also follows in those struck. Straton — who records what has been said above about this creature and about those struck by it — also said that this creature leaps especially at the testicles, not only of men, but of every animal.

These too are helped, since they are also at risk of putrefaction, with the general remedies and, further, as follows: give tender bay-leaves ground fine with wine to drink; give southernwood boiled in wine to drink, and wild thyme likewise; give galbanum dissolved in wine to drink; give tender cypress-balls with wine to drink; and apply an equal amount of cyclamen with oil as a poultice to the bites, anointing the surrounding areas as well.

If the wound bursts open, bathe it with vinegar-brine. Once it ulcerates, apply a poultice of boiled sweet pomegranate, and bathe with a decoction of myrtle; galbanum applied as a compress over the bite also helps, as does barley-meal with oxymel applied as a poultice; a bite from the very same creature that inflicted the wound serves as its own antidote; and pellitory sprinkled onto the wound also helps.

Archigenes, in his books On Remedies by Kind, says: in those bitten by the shrew there follows throbbing pain, redness at each tooth-puncture, and blisters full of serum, with serous discharges; once a blister is completely stripped away, the flesh beneath appears at the ulcer, which, as it is scraped, breaks down into sinewy membranes; and sometimes, in addition, putrefied portions of flesh fall away.

Those bitten are helped by drinking, right away, the shrew itself ground up in wine, or horehound, or rocket, or cultivated safflower, or mint, or southernwood, or the other remedies described for similar cases.

div.head: The Chalcidian lizard and the salamander
div.p: In those struck by the Chalcidian lizard, as I found recorded in the work of Soranus, along with the bite there occurs a translucent swelling...

In those struck by the Chalcidian lizard there occurs a translucent swelling, as if lit from within like a lamp, and a blackening of the area, and putrefaction; and so these too should be treated with the remedies described for the shrew-bite.
In those struck by the salamander there occurs severe surrounding pain and the formation of a scab. Here too the treatment should be proportioned to the symptoms that follow.

div.head: Four-jawed creatures and spiders
div.p: There are two kinds of four-jawed creatures: one is somewhat flat and whitish, has rough legs, and on the head two projections, one straight and one slanted, so that it appears to have two mouths and four jaws. The other, as the writers on venomous creatures have described it, has an even, thin line resembling a mouth, so that it too seems to have two mouths and four jaws.

In those struck by these creatures, as Archigenes says in his work On Remedies by Kind, the same symptoms generally follow, along with dimming of vision; but peculiar to them are these: the sting hurts intensely, the area around it turns somewhat white, sleeplessness occurs, there is a sensation running through the face and head, and sometimes the struck limbs waste away as far as the joints, remaining wasted even once healed.
They are helped by drinking calamint, or trefoil, or rue, or all-heal, or poley-germander, and by the remedies described for spider-bites, for these too are a kind of spider.

There is also a certain kind of spider that, when it strikes, brings severe pains around the middle of the flank, redness, and difficulty urinating, sometimes also a choking sensation. Those struck by these are helped by drinking wild Theban cumin, or chaste-tree seed, or the leaves of the white poplar, or by taking large amounts of garlic while sipping unmixed wine. Apollonius too, in his Useful Remedies, hands down to us nearly the same remedies, advising that garlic be given with meals, along with chaste-tree cumin taken with unmixed wine.

div.head: The toad
div.p: Theodorus, in his own treatise on the toad, explaining to us both its appearance and its nature, speaks as follows: the toad seems to me to be a kind of frog, a creature living in water, but changed from its marsh-dwelling nature to a land-dwelling one.

It is called phrynos similarly to the chersydros, and it inflicts injury that is hard to heal on those who encounter it: for the creature is of considerable size, not much smaller than a small tortoise; its back grows rough, and it swells greatly when its breath is provoked to anger.

It defends itself boldly against whatever confronts it, and by its leaps closes the distance between itself and its target, though it rarely resorts to biting. Its breath is by nature such as to produce a venomous effect, so that merely being near it when it breathes harms those close by. I pass over the many other things recorded about this creature, being concerned to set down only the more useful matters.

In those struck by it there follows swelling of the whole body, a breaking-down of the tissues, and swift death. The remedies to be applied in these cases should be drawn from what has been handed down above — that is, the universal and general antidotes, and the rest of the appropriate diet.

div.head: Sea sting-rays and moray-eels
div.p: In those struck by the sea sting-ray, the wound is plainly visible, and violent pain sets in at once, together with numbness over the whole body, putrefaction, and swift death. Some record that if the ray's spine is removed after it has struck and fixed into a tree, especially...

Those struck by it are helped, since chill and numbness follow over the whole body, by warming ointments and the other general poultices. Specifically for these cases, boiled bran should be applied to the bites, and vinegar by itself helps a great deal.

Straton, for his part, hands down to us the following: the same symptoms follow as in viper-bites, and so similar remedies should be used. Archigenes says: for the various kinds of sea creatures — the sting-ray, the moray-eel, the sea-dragon — give four or five drops of fig-sap together with three or four sprigs of wild thyme to drink.
